notes.text: Pathology mechanisms in clinical vignettes
Ionizing radiation can injure cells through reactive oxygen species generated from water.
Ubiquitin tagging directs proteins toward proteasomal degradation during muscle wasting.
Coagulative necrosis typifies ischemia in many solid organs; brain infarction instead undergoes liquefactive necrosis.
Pressure overload enlarges cardiomyocytes through hypertrophy.

notes.text: Cell death and tissue response
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Necrosis involves loss of membrane integrity and commonly provokes inflammation.
Apoptosis is regulated cell death with cellular fragmentation and clearance of apoptotic bodies.
Coagulative necrosis preserves tissue architecture initially and is typical of ischemic injury in most solid organs other than the brain.
Liquefactive necrosis is associated with brain infarction and many bacterial abscesses.
Caseous necrosis has a granular, cheese-like appearance and is classically associated with tuberculosis.

title: Intracellular Accumulations: Mechanism of Accumulation & Types- Lipids, Proteins, Carbon, Lipofuscin

notes.text: Why material accumulates in cells
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Steatosis is the accumulation of triglycerides within cells, especially hepatocytes.
Lipofuscin is a residual pigment associated with lipid peroxidation and cellular aging.
Hemosiderin stores iron and can be demonstrated with a Prussian blue stain.
Carbon particles may be retained in macrophages after inhalation; impaired clearance can produce tissue deposits.

title: Amyloidosis: Classification, Appearance on Histological Slides, Clinical Features & Diagnosis

notes.text: Amyloid deposition
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Amyloid consists of extracellular deposits of misfolded proteins with a beta-pleated sheet configuration.
Congo red staining produces characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
AL amyloid is derived from immunoglobulin light chains and can accompany plasma-cell disorders.
AA amyloid derives from serum amyloid A and is associated with chronic inflammatory disease.

title: Oxidative Stress (Free Radical Injury): Physiologic & Pathologic Generation, Elimination & Examples

notes.text: Oxidative injury
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Reactive oxygen species can damage membrane lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide.
Catalase and glutathione peroxidase participate in hydrogen peroxide removal.
Reperfusion can intensify injury through oxidant generation and inflammatory activation after ischemia.

title: Cell Injury: Definition, Causes (Ischemia, Hypoxemia, Decrease O2 Carrying Capacity) and Features

notes.text: Mechanisms of cell injury
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Hypoxemia means reduced oxygen in arterial blood; it is distinct from reduced tissue perfusion.
Ischemia limits oxygen and nutrient delivery while impairing removal of metabolic waste.
ATP depletion impairs ion pumps and can produce cellular swelling.
Irreversible injury is associated with severe mitochondrial dysfunction and loss of membrane integrity.

title: Cellular Adaptations (Growth Adaptations): Hypertrophy, Hyperplasia, Atrophy, Metaplasia

notes.text: Adaptation versus injury
A concise, newly authored revision guide for this topic. Use the video for the instructor’s full explanation; these notes do not claim to transcribe it.
Hypertrophy means an increase in cell size.
Hyperplasia means an increase in cell number in a tissue capable of proliferation.
Atrophy means a reduction in cell size and sometimes cell number.
Metaplasia is replacement of one differentiated cell type by another better suited to a persistent stress.
